statement: Backward recursion is the dynamic programming procedure that determines the optimal value function and optimal policy by breaking a multi-stage decision problem into recursive sub-problems and solving the Bellman recurrence relation backwards from terminal boundary conditions: for a discrete system at the k-th stage of n intervals, J_k^*(x_{n-k}) = min_{u_{n-k}} { f_hat(x_{n-k}, u_{n-k}) + J_{k-1}^*(g_hat(x_{n-k}, u_{n-k})) } (or V_t(k_t) = max_{c_t} { ln(c_t) + b * V_{t+1}(k_{t+1}) }), initialized by terminal boundary condition J_0^*(x_n) = b(x(t_1), t_1) (or V_{T+1} = 0). Computing sequentially backwards from V_i yields V_{i-1} until reaching initial state V_1 (or V_0), after which optimal decision variables are recovered one by one by tracking back.

symbols.meaning: discrete system state vector at stage n-k
discrete approximation of system transition dynamics
optimal cost-to-go at the k-th backward stage
terminal boundary cost function in control theory, or discount factor in Ramsey saving problem
initial and terminal continuous time bounds
value function representing optimal remaining value at time t
consumption choice variable at time t
capital stock state variable at time t

steps.text: A dynamic optimization problem spanning multiple points in time is broken down into recursive sub-problems. If the problem can be solved optimally by combining optimal solutions to sub-problems, it possesses optimal substructure, formulated in continuous control as minimizing J = b(x(t_1), t_1) + int_{t_0}^{t_1} f(x(t), u(t), t) dt subject to dx/dt = g(x(t), u(t), t), or in discrete time as maximizing sum_{t=0}^T b^t ln(c_t) subject to k_{t+1} = A k_t^a - c_t >= 0.

Decompose the sequential decision process by defining a sequence of value functions (cost-to-go functions) that represent the optimal value of being in any state at each time. For continuous control, the optimal policy u^* = h(x(t), t) yields cost-to-go function J^*(x(t), t) with boundary condition J(t_1) = b(x(t_1), t_1). For discrete time, define value functions V_t(k) for t = 0, 1, ..., T+1, with terminal condition V_{T+1}(k) = 0 representing zero utility after the terminal horizon.

Express the stage-to-stage transition via the Bellman recurrence relation. Approximating the continuous control process by a discrete system of n equally spaced intervals yields the recurrence relation analog to the Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman equation at the k-th stage: J_k^*(x_{n-k}) = min_{u_{n-k}} { f_hat(x_{n-k}, u_{n-k}) + J_{k-1}^*(g_hat(x_{n-k}, u_{n-k})) }. Analogously, for discrete Ramsey savings, the Bellman equation is V_t(k_t) = max { ln(c_t) + b * V_{t+1}(k_{t+1}) } subject to k_{t+1} = A k_t^a - c_t >= 0.

Solve the recurrence relation backwards from the terminal boundary condition. Initializing with known terminal value V_{T+1}(k) = 0 (or stage k = 0 with J_0^*(x_n) = b(x(t_1), t_1)), application of the Bellman equation yields V_T(k) (or J_1^*). In general, once V_{T-j+1}(k) (or V_i) has already been calculated for the needed states, the operation yields V_{T-j}(k) (or V_{i-1}) by solving V_{T-j}(k) = max_{c_{T-j}} { ln(c_{T-j}) + b * V_{T-j+1}(A k^a - c_{T-j}) }, iterating backwards until reaching V_0(k) (or V_1 at the initial state).

Recover the optimal trajectory and decision variables by tracking back the calculations already performed from the initial state forward, giving closed-form optimal consumption c_{T-j}(k) = (1 / sum_{i=0}^j a^i b^i) A k^a, simplifying from c_T(k) = A k^a to c_0(k) = (A k^a) / (1 + ab + ... + a^T b^T).

assumptions.assumption: Optimal substructure: an optimal solution to the overall optimization problem is composed of optimal solutions to its recursive sub-problems.
assumptions.breaks_when: Decisions cannot be separated recursively across time points, or path costs depend globally on trajectory history in a non-separable manner.

assumptions.assumption: Overlapping sub-problems: the sub-problem state space is small enough that intermediate solutions can be tabulated and reused.
assumptions.breaks_when: Sub-problems do not overlap (reducing to divide-and-conquer) or state space is continuous without a valid discrete approximation, leading to an intractable state space.

assumptions.assumption: Known terminal boundary condition: the terminal cost or valuation at the end of the horizon is well-defined and known (e.g., J(t_1) = b(x(t_1), t_1) or V_{T+1}(k) = 0).
assumptions.breaks_when: The planning horizon is undefined or terminal value is unknown or unbounded without convergence.

assumptions.assumption: Feasible state transitions: admissible controls exist such that state trajectories satisfy system transition constraints at every backward stage.
assumptions.breaks_when: State constraints become infeasible (e.g., k_{t+1} = A k_t^a - c_t < 0 when capital is constrained to be non-negative).

failure_modes.signature: Exponential computational complexity and memory exhaustion when computing J_k^*(x_{n-k}) across state grids.
failure_modes.cause: High-dimensional continuous state and control spaces require fine discretization grids whose size grows exponentially with dimension.

failure_modes.mode: Sub-problem non-separability / lack of optimal substructure
failure_modes.signature: Backward recursive solution fails to achieve the global optimum of the original problem.
failure_modes.cause: The objective function or constraints couple decision variables across time in a way that cannot be factored into stage-wise Bellman transitions.

failure_modes.signature: Calculated value functions V_t and recovered controls systematically diverge from true optimal values.
failure_modes.cause: Incorrectly assigned terminal boundary value b(x(t_1), t_1) or V_{T+1}, which propagates errors backward through every stage.

failure_modes.mode: State constraint violation / empty control set
failure_modes.signature: Optimization at stage n-k or time t returns no feasible solution.
failure_modes.cause: Preceding choices or state transitions force the state into a region where the admissible control constraint set is empty (e.g., A k_t^a - c_t < 0).
